items.title: Impressionist beauty ideals aligned with modern clinical classifications of obesity
items.summary:
Researchers recently estimated the body mass index of female figures depicted in 19th-century Impressionist paintings, finding that these historical beauty ideals align with modern clinical classifications of obesity. The shifting standards highlight a stark contrast between past cultural preferences for fuller body types and contemporary pressures to achieve extreme thinness. The study was published in the International Journal of Obesity .

Throughout history, societies have continually redefined female beauty. Human aesthetic preferences are frequently tied to specific cultural values and the societal roles women are expected to fulfill. In the Paleolithic era, artifacts like the Venus of Willendorf featured prominent abdomens and ample breasts. These physical traits were celebrated as symbols of fertility and the ability to sustain life. During the Renaissance and Baroque periods, artists continued to emphasize voluptuous forms, associating rounded bodies with abundance and sensuality.

By the late 19th century, the Industrial Revolution had profoundly altered the world. Women began moving away from agricultural labor and domestic roles, increasingly participating in paid factory work within urban environments. Despite these shifting social structures, artistic representations of women remained anchored to classical ideals. Impressionist painters continued to feature soft, rounded forms as the epitome of feminine beauty.

This artistic preference for fuller shapes stood in sharp contrast to the lived reality of the general population. Economic hardship and widespread…
items.t: Impressionist beauty ideals aligned with modern clinical classifications of obesity

items.title: Dopamine cells slow the heart during danger, new fruit fly research indicates
items.summary:
Researchers have identified four dopamine-producing brain cells in fruit flies that briefly slow the insect’s heartbeat when it encounters a sudden physical threat. Published in eLife , the study indicates that these same four nerve cells also spur the fly to spend more time walking in response to danger. When the scientists bypassed the brain and used light pulses to slow the heart muscle directly, walking increased as well, suggesting that changes in heart rhythm may help shape escape behavior.

Brain and heart signals travel in both directions 
 Dopaminergic neurons are nerve cells in the brain that communicate by releasing dopamine, a chemical messenger involved in movement, motivation, and sensory processing. In the new work, scientists examined how a small set of these cells links threat processing in the brain to the fruit fly’s heart. That organ is a muscular tube made of two rows of contracting cells running along the midline of the abdomen, lined with nerve connections.

Across the animal kingdom, encountering danger triggers coordinated shifts in behavior and pulse rate. In mammals, detecting a threat often causes a brief slowing of the heartbeat, which researchers propose may quiet heartbeat-related signals in the brain to sharpen sensory attention. A faster pulse typically follows to supply muscles with energy during active escape.

Specialized brain circuits direct many of these cardiovascular reactions from the top down. For example, an experiment in marmoset monkeys found that over-activating a frontal region called the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex…
items.t: Dopamine cells slow the heart during danger, new fruit fly research indicates

items.title: Eating more fruits and vegetables is linked to a lower risk of depression
items.summary:
People who consume higher amounts of fruits and vegetables may face a lower risk of developing depression over time. A massive review of observational research found that eating more produce is consistently linked to better mental health outcomes, suggesting that diet could play a role in preventing depressive disorders. The findings were published in the Journal of Affective Disorders .

Depression affects millions of people globally and represents a leading cause of disability. Mental health professionals have increasingly looked at daily lifestyle habits, such as nutrition, to find ways to reduce the risk of mood disorders. Fruits and vegetables contain vitamins, fiber, and compounds called antioxidants that help protect the brain and body from cellular damage. This cellular damage is known as oxidative stress.

High fiber intake also supports the gut microbiome, which is the community of bacteria living in the digestive tract. Certain types of dietary fiber act as prebiotics, feeding these beneficial bacteria. A healthier gut microbiome can reduce widespread inflammation in the body, which has been increasingly identified as a biological contributor to depressive disorders. These bacteria communicate with the brain through the gut-brain axis, a biological pathway that influences the production of mood-regulating chemicals like serotonin.

Previous research on diet and depression has yielded mixed results. Some prior studies only focused on specific age groups, like younger adults, where the protective association appeared weaker. Other research looked mainly at…
items.t: Eating more fruits and vegetables is linked to a lower risk of depression

items.title: Muscle dysmorphia symptoms linked to a range of sexual difficulties in young men
items.summary:
Boys and young men who experience stronger symptoms of muscle dysmorphia tend to report a wider array of sexual difficulties, according to new research published in Body Image . Across nearly all aspects of sexual health examined, intense dissatisfaction and anxiety over physical appearance stood out as the symptom dimension most consistently tied to trouble during sex. The findings suggest that health professionals supporting young men with body image concerns may also want to consider their sexual well-being.

Muscle dysmorphia is a mental health condition classified as a form of body dysmorphic disorder, an illness marked by obsessive distress over perceived flaws in how one looks. People with muscle dysmorphia become preoccupied with the belief that their bodies are too small or insufficiently muscular, even when they have average or above-average muscle mass, and often follow rigid weightlifting schedules or strict diets that disrupt their daily lives. Prior surveys indicate that roughly 26% of adolescent boys and young men in a Canadian community sample reported clinically meaningful muscle dysmorphia symptoms, while 25% to 26% of their peers in the United States reported engaging in muscle-building behaviors such as weightlifting, supplement use, or steroid use.

Prior work has linked muscle dysmorphia symptoms to depression, anxiety, substance use, and suicidal thoughts, prompting researchers to ask whether these struggles extend to sexual health. Sexual difficulties such as trouble maintaining an erection, performance anxiety, and low desire affect anywhere from…
items.t: Muscle dysmorphia symptoms linked to a range of sexual difficulties in young men

items.title: Musically trained children score higher on tests of intelligence, working memory, and reading
items.summary:
A study of 7- to 9-year-olds found that children who regularly practiced a musical instrument tended to score higher on tests of cognitive ability and academic achievement than children without musical training. Brain scans also hinted at a difference in a right-hemisphere white matter pathway connecting auditory and motor regions, though this finding was not statistically robust. The paper was published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience .

Childhood is an important period of brain development, during which environmental experiences can influence the structure and functioning of the brain. Participating in extracurricular activities, such as learning to play a musical instrument, may contribute to children’s cognitive development.

Research has found that musical training can improve music-related abilities, such as recognizing rhythms and melodies, but its benefits may also extend to non-musical skills. Studies have reported improvements in executive functioning, reading comprehension, language abilities, and academic performance among children who received musical training. Some studies have also found that these improvements are accompanied by changes in brain activity and connectivity.

Researchers have used brain imaging techniques to investigate how musical training relates to the structure of white matter, which consists of nerve fibers connecting different brain regions. Of particular interest is the arcuate fasciculus, a bundle of nerve fibers connecting brain regions involved in language, auditory processing, and related functions. Previous research has…
items.t: Musically trained children score higher on tests of intelligence, working memory, and reading

items.title: Supernatural delusions are common in psychedelic-linked killings, studies find
items.summary:
A pair of new studies examining rare homicides committed under the influence of psychedelic drugs indicates that sudden breaks with reality and false beliefs about imminent danger frequently drive these fatal attacks. One study, published in Journal of Police and Criminal Psychology , analyzed statistical and thematic patterns across more than 600 cases.

A companion study in Psychiatry, Psychology and Law profiled 22 individual offenders in detail, indicating along with the broader analysis that delusion-driven killings often target loved ones without prior hostility and result in starkly different prison sentences across countries.

Psychedelics, psychosis, and criminal responsibility 
 Classic psychedelics are mind-altering drugs, including lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), psilocybin from “magic mushrooms,” mescaline, and dimethyltryptamine (DMT, the main active ingredient in the plant brew ayahuasca), that temporarily alter perception, mood, and thought. Clinical research into their mental health benefits and recreational use have both grown rapidly, and severe emergencies remain rare: a large international survey of magic mushroom users found that only 0.2 percent of past-year users sought emergency medical treatment, mostly for short-lived panic or anxiety that resolved within 24 hours.

Population-level data have even linked certain psychedelics to lower crime rates, as a national survey analysis of U.S. adults found that lifetime psilocybin use was associated with lower statistical odds of ever having been arrested, while LSD showed no statistical association with…
items.t: Supernatural delusions are common in psychedelic-linked killings, studies find

items.title: Republicans experience worse mental health in Democratic neighborhoods, study finds
items.summary:
Republicans living in neighborhoods dominated by Democrats experience worse mental health than those residing in heavily Republican areas. Democrats, on the other hand, report similar levels of anxiety, depression, and loneliness regardless of the political makeup of their communities. These findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences .

Politics in the United States functions as a powerful social identity that extends beyond voting. Past research shows that a person’s neighborhood can influence who they interact with, what they buy, and even their physical health decisions. A team of political scientists and medical researchers wanted to see if the political alignment between a person and their neighbors might also be linked to psychological well-being.

The research was conducted by Ryan Baxter-King of the University of Nevada, Reno, alongside colleagues from Boston University, Harvard University, and the University of California, Los Angeles. They utilized a large survey of 165,000 adults conducted between May 2020 and December 2022. The researchers combined this survey data with national voter registration records to determine the exact proportion of Democrats and Republicans in each respondent’s Zip Code.

To measure mental health, the survey relied on established clinical questionnaires. Depression was evaluated using an eight-question scale that looks for standard symptoms of major depressive disorder. Anxiety was measured using a four-item scale developed for patient-reported outcomes, and loneliness was assessed with questions…
items.t: Republicans experience worse mental health in Democratic neighborhoods, study finds

items.title: Family ties emerge as a key link between poverty and teen well-being in Taiwanese study
items.summary:
A study of more than 1,300 Taiwanese adolescents living in poverty found that their relationships with family members, teachers, and peers may help explain the link between material deprivation and substance use. Family relationships also appeared to play a role in the link between material deprivation and psychological distress. The paper was published in Behavioral Sciences & the Law .

Adolescence is an important developmental period during which young people frequently experience psychological distress and some engage in problematic behaviors such as substance use. These problems can negatively affect their academic performance, relationships, health, and overall well-being, potentially leading to difficulties later in life.

One factor associated with these problems is material deprivation, a lack of essential resources such as food, clothing, electricity, medical care, or money for everyday needs. Adolescents experiencing material deprivation may face increased distress, and some may turn to substance use as a way of coping. However, previous studies have produced mixed findings, with some suggesting that material deprivation may actually limit substance use because adolescents cannot afford alcohol, cigarettes, or drugs.

Another important factor is the quality of adolescents’ relationships with family members, peers, and teachers, which may influence how they respond to material hardship. Poor social relationships may increase feelings of isolation, emotional difficulties, and the likelihood of engaging in substance use.

Study authors Zewei Liu and Ji-Kang Chen of…
items.t: Family ties emerge as a key link between poverty and teen well-being in Taiwanese study

items.title: Psychologists map the connection between dark personality traits and romantic jealousy
items.summary:
New research suggests that aggressive personality traits in romantic relationships often express themselves through an obsessive, possessive approach to love, which in turn feeds intense jealousy. Published in Sexual and Relationship Therapy , the dual-study investigation reveals that an individual’s specific style of loving acts as a psychological bridge between antagonistic tendencies and jealous reactions. The findings offer a deeper look at how some people navigate relationship threats and manage intimate bonds.

In the 1970s, psychologist John Alan Lee proposed a framework for understanding how different people experience romantic love. He categorized love into six distinct styles. Eros represents a passionate, immediate attraction akin to love at first sight. Ludus treats love as a game, often involving manipulation and a focus on short-term pleasure without deep commitment. Storge is built on friendship, valuing stability, trust, and mutual respect.

The remaining three styles blend the primary orientations. Pragma combines elements of Ludus and Storge, taking a highly practical approach to finding a partner who meets specific criteria. Mania blends Eros and Ludus into an obsessive, possessive, and emotionally volatile experience. Agape mixes Eros and Storge, resulting in a selfless, compassionate orientation where one prioritizes the partner’s needs without expecting anything in return.

Lead author Bruno Bonfa-Araujo, a psychology researcher at the Universidade Tuiuti do Parana in Brazil, and his colleagues wanted to understand how these love styles relate to…
items.t: Psychologists map the connection between dark personality traits and romantic jealousy

items.title: Brain differences in dyslexia appear before children learn to read
items.summary:
Children who later develop dyslexia already show subtle differences in how a visual-language brain region responds to repeated written words in kindergarten, before formal reading lessons begin, according to a longitudinal study published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience . At the same time, they process repeated faces, houses, and objects much like their peers, suggesting that early brain differences in dyslexia are tied to print rather than reflecting a general difficulty adapting to repeated sights.

Dyslexia is a learning condition marked by persistent difficulty reading accurately and fluently despite typical intelligence and adequate instruction. One proposed explanation involves neural adaptation, in which brain cells respond less intensely when a person sees or hears the same item repeatedly compared to encountering different items. That drop in activity reflects how efficiently a brain region recognizes familiar patterns and tunes itself to specific categories.

Support for that idea came from a 2016 neuroimaging study of adults and school-age children , which found weaker neural adaptation in adults with dyslexia across repeated spoken words, written words, faces, and objects, and in children with dyslexia for spoken words. Those authors proposed that a broad failure to adapt rapidly to repeated input might be a core cause of dyslexia rather than a consequence, though later studies in adults and older children yielded mixed results.

All of those earlier studies shared a major catch: every participant already knew how to read. Because people with dyslexia…
items.t: Brain differences in dyslexia appear before children learn to read

items.title: New study finds children and teens reason differently about participation trophies
items.summary:
Children as young as 7 and teenagers largely agree that reserving trophies for top finishers motivates athletes to try harder and feel prouder than handing out participation awards to everyone, according to a new study published in Developmental Science . Yet only adolescents consistently predicted negative side effects from winner-only awards, expecting them to encourage cheating and physical risk-taking. Teenagers’ personal preferences for competitive versus inclusive trophy systems also aligned with how fast they believed they could run, suggesting that self-interest begins shaping views on fairness by adolescence.

At the end of many youth sports seasons, leagues choose between two competing rules for handing out awards. Inclusive, or egalitarian, reward systems give every participant the same recognition simply for showing up and taking part, whereas selective, or merit-based, systems reserve prizes for top performers based on measurable results.

Supporters of participation trophies argue that inclusive recognition fosters belonging and acknowledges effort, while critics contend that giving everyone the same prize dilutes achievement and dulls motivation. Selective trophies spark parallel disagreements between advocates who see them as fair recognition for excellence and critics who worry they create pressure to take unethical shortcuts or risk injury.

“Although these debates largely take place among adults, children are the ones who experience these reward systems,” study lead author Shuai Shao , who conducted the research at the University of California, San…
items.t: New study finds children and teens reason differently about participation trophies

items.title: The right message can shift support for universal basic income across party lines
items.summary:
Framing universal basic income around core moral beliefs about social equality and family tradition can shift Americans’ attitudes toward the policy across party lines, according to new research published in American Politics Research . A national survey experiment indicates that people’s underlying personal values, rather than their political party labels alone, guide whether they accept or reject arguments for guaranteed government cash payments. Republicans who personally value equality became more favorable toward the policy when it was framed as advancing that value, though that result rested on a handful of respondents.

Universal basic income, often abbreviated as UBI, is a social policy proposal in which the government sends regular, unconditional cash payments to every adult citizen, regardless of their income, employment status, or financial need. A number of American cities have tested smaller guaranteed income pilot programs in recent years, yet the idea faces stiff resistance at the national level, particularly among Republicans and conservatives who generally oppose expanding government spending.

Political scientists have debated whether changing how the policy is framed, meaning emphasizing certain aspects or consequences of an issue in public messaging, can overcome this partisan divide. In a 2021 survey experiment by three of the same authors, neither factual policy details nor broad value appeals persuaded Americans to cross party lines on basic income.

Similarly, a 2022 experimental study of American adults found that pitching universal basic income…
items.t: The right message can shift support for universal basic income across party lines

items.title: Steroid users face triple the risk of long-term erectile dysfunction
items.summary:
Men who use anabolic steroids to build muscle and enhance athletic performance face a substantially higher risk of experiencing long-term erectile dysfunction compared to non-users. In the years after being sanctioned for steroid use, steroid users were three times more likely to require prescription medications to treat impotence. The findings were published in The Journal of Sexual Medicine .

Anabolic-androgenic steroids are synthetic variations of the male sex hormone testosterone. Doctors occasionally prescribe these drugs to treat specific medical conditions, such as delayed puberty or diseases that cause muscle loss. Outside of medical settings, athletes and bodybuilders often use these substances to increase muscle mass, reduce fat, and improve their physical performance. 

While steroids are heavily associated with competitive sports, their use extends deep into the general population. Current estimates suggest that about six percent of men worldwide will use anabolic steroids at some point in their lives.

Using synthetic hormones comes with severe biological consequences. The human body relies on a delicate biological system known as the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis to regulate hormone production. This system operates on a negative feedback loop. When the brain detects that there is enough testosterone in the bloodstream, it stops sending signals to the testicles to produce more.

When a person introduces large amounts of artificial testosterone into their system through steroid use, the brain senses the hormone overload. The brain immediately shuts down…
items.t: Steroid users face triple the risk of long-term erectile dysfunction

items.title: Common genetic variants matter more in Alzheimer’s than scientists thought
items.summary:
An international genetic study of more than 2.8 million people has identified 127 regions of human DNA associated with Alzheimer’s disease, including 48 regions linked to the condition for the first time.

Published in Nature , the research indicates that common inherited variants account for nearly three times as much of the population variation in Alzheimer’s risk as previous estimates suggested. The findings also connect genetic susceptibility to heightened gene activity in brain immune cells alongside dampened gene activity in nerve cells.

Searching for Missing Genetic Risk in Alzheimer’s Disease 
 Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive brain disorder that gradually erodes memory, reasoning, and everyday functioning, accounting for most dementia cases worldwide. Existing disease-modifying drugs mainly aim to remove sticky clumps of amyloid-beta protein from brain tissue, yet they tend to offer modest symptom relief. Because twin studies indicate that inherited differences account for 60% to 80% of the variation in Alzheimer’s risk, researchers use genome-wide association studies, scanning millions of common single-letter DNA variations across populations to find chromosomal regions, called loci, linked to the illness.

Larger samples have steadily expanded that map. For example, a 2021 genetic study of more than 1.1 million people was led by several of the same researchers, including co-lead author Douglas Wightman, and shared several cohorts with the new work. That analysis uncovered seven new risk regions and highlighted microglia, the specialized immune cells in the…
items.t: Common genetic variants matter more in Alzheimer’s than scientists thought

items.title: New research finds a surprising downside to bodily synchrony between strangers
items.summary:
Falling into physical sync with someone else is widely assumed to encourage generosity and cooperation, yet a new study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B suggests that matching bodily responses can sometimes point in the opposite direction. When pairs of strangers played an unequal game of financial trust, partners whose sweat responses rose and fell together saw smaller returns sent back to the person who took the initial risk, but only when the two could see each other. The findings indicate that sweat synchrony is not automatically cooperative, and that its social effects depend on both visual contact and a partner’s level of emotional engagement.

During social interactions, two people often begin to mirror each other’s automatic bodily processes, a phenomenon known as physiological synchrony. Without either person noticing, involuntary signals such as heart rate or microscopic sweating can rise and fall on nearly the same schedule. Scientists frequently measure it through skin conductance, which tracks tiny changes in how easily the skin carries a mild electrical current as sweat glands react to emotional arousal and alertness.

“The mechanism behind this is still unknown, but this happens all the time – between mothers and their children, between romantic or friend couples, between therapist and patient,” study lead author Fabiola Diana , who conducted the research at Leiden University and Utrecht University and is now a postdoctoral researcher at ETH Zurich , told PsyPost. “Years of research on this topic have shown that synchrony is supposed to make…
items.t: New research finds a surprising downside to bodily synchrony between strangers

items.title: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson
items.summary:
As teenagers, my friends and I thought it was glamorous to have relationships with older men. But after the revelations about Russell Brand and David Walliams, I have started to see that period of my life in a new light

It has been a strange time to be a “woman of a certain age”, as Gregg Wallace so charmingly labelled us. Many of us were consumed by every detail of the Russell Brand trial and the David Walliams exposé. We were pleasantly surprised, albeit dazed – stunned even – by there being consequences for their behaviour, because that’s not how it usually goes, in our experience.

A few days ago, while spending time with a group of fellow certain-agers, among whom this was the main topic of discussion, as it has been pretty much everywhere I’ve been, I confessed to something of which I’m ashamed. If I had been the woman Brand was found guilty of raping – in an attack that was difficult even to read about – I worry that I would have felt powerless to complain about what had happened. I would have thought consent would be taken as a blanket statement that covered whatever followed, however horrifying and unwanted; that I’d made my bed, so was obliged to lie in it, come what may.…
items.t: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson

items.title: Unwavering cooperators make group efforts easier to start but harder to sustain
items.summary:
A small band of unconditionally cooperative individuals can make it much easier for a group to get a shared effort off the ground, yet their reliability may also encourage others to slack off over the long run. According to a new mathematical modeling study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B , unwavering cooperators act as a double-edged sword in group tasks that require a minimum number of contributors to succeed. The findings suggest that committed minorities can help spark collective action while simultaneously reducing overall participation once coordination takes hold.

Cooperation allows living things, from bacteria building protective films to humans funding public infrastructure, to achieve together what no single individual could manage alone. Yet pitching in carries a personal cost in time, energy, or resources, leaving contributors vulnerable to free-riders who enjoy the shared benefits without doing any of the work.

To study when helpful behavior survives or dies out under these pressures, scientists often turn to evolutionary game theory, a mathematical framework that tracks how competing strategies spread or shrink in a population depending on the payoffs they earn. Even in anonymous, one-time encounters where people cannot reward helpers or punish slackers, outcomes can shift in the presence of what game theorists call zealots: committed individuals who always cooperate and never change their strategy, regardless of what others do.

Earlier research suggested that a small fraction of these steadfast contributors could nudge an entire group…
items.t: Unwavering cooperators make group efforts easier to start but harder to sustain

items.title: Popular cannabis supplement shows inconsistent anti-inflammatory effects in brain cells
items.summary:
Cannabigerol, a non-intoxicating compound from the cannabis plant, has gained popularity as a dietary supplement for its purported anti-inflammatory and brain-protecting properties. However, new laboratory research published in Toxicology suggests that its effects on brain immune cells are inconsistent and heavily dependent on concentration. Low doses left cells intact, yet all but the smallest broke isolated DNA in a cell-free test. The highest concentration killed cells and triggered severe chemical stress, and lower doses failed to reliably calm an induced inflammatory response.

Cannabigerol is a naturally occurring chemical belonging to a class of molecules called phytocannabinoids, which are produced by the Cannabis sativa plant. Unlike tetrahydrocannabinol, the primary compound responsible for the cannabis “high,” cannabigerol does not cause intoxication or impair coordination, making it an attractive candidate for everyday supplements and potential therapies. Early human research has added to that interest, including a placebo-controlled trial in adults that found taking 20 milligrams of hemp-derived cannabigerol reduced feelings of anxiety and stress and modestly improved verbal memory recall compared to a placebo.

Beyond mood and memory, scientists have investigated whether cannabigerol can protect the nervous system from neuroinflammation, a persistent immune response inside the brain and spinal cord that contributes to neurodegenerative illnesses. Brain immunity is managed primarily by microglia, specialized immune cells residing in neural tissue that sweep up…
items.t: Popular cannabis supplement shows inconsistent anti-inflammatory effects in brain cells

items.title: People who feel humiliated tend to be less happy, and rumination may partly explain why
items.summary:
An online survey conducted in Poland found that people who reported more humiliation, including both past humiliating experiences and fear of being humiliated in the future, tended to be less happy and more prone to rumination. Statistical analyses suggested that rumination partly accounted for the link between humiliation and lower happiness. The paper was published in Current Issues in Personality Psychology .

Humiliation is a distressing experience that can leave vivid, lasting memories and negatively affect how people see themselves and their relationships with others. It has been linked to lower self-esteem, impaired concentration, disrupted relationships, emotional distress, and depression, and dwelling on humiliating experiences may even motivate aggressive behavior.

A related psychological phenomenon is rumination, which involves repetitive negative thinking about distressing experiences, personal concerns, and fears. Rumination can prolong and intensify negative emotions, interfere with cognitive functioning, and make it more difficult to recover from upsetting experiences.

Both humiliation and rumination may reduce a person’s happiness, understood here as overall well-being and satisfaction with one’s life. Humiliation and rumination may also interfere with posttraumatic growth, a process through which individuals experience positive psychological changes following adversity.

items.t: People who feel humiliated tend to be less happy, and rumination may partly explain why

items.title: New case study offers causal evidence linking the right amygdala to PTSD
items.summary:
In a rare clinical case involving a man with drug-resistant epilepsy and severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), selectively inactivating part of his right amygdala reduced his tendency to perceive ambiguous faces as fearful and was followed by a sharp drop in trauma symptoms. Published in Nature Communications , the study tracked brain signals and emotion perception before and immediately after the awake bedside procedure. Although drawn from a single patient, the findings offer unusual causal evidence that right-amygdala activity helps sustain threat-focused biases and PTSD symptoms.

Threat bias and the amygdala in PTSD 
 PTSD is a psychiatric condition that can develop after severe trauma, marked by intrusive memories, avoidance of trauma reminders, negative shifts in mood and thinking, and persistent physical jumpiness. A central feature of the disorder is negative interpretation bias, the tendency to read neutral or ambiguous cues, such as an unreadable facial expression, as threatening. Seeing everyday surroundings as dangerous keeps fear responses active and makes emotions harder to regulate.

Research into this threat bias often focuses on the amygdala, a pair of almond-shaped neuron clusters deep inside the brain’s left and right temporal lobes, roughly behind the temples. The amygdala helps detect danger and coordinate fear responses, and brain scans consistently show heightened amygdala reactivity to fearful or neutral sights in people with PTSD. items.t: New case study offers causal evidence linking the right amygdala to PTSD

items.title: People tend to underestimate how much they get in the way of their partner’s goals
items.summary:
People in cohabiting relationships often knew when they were helping or hindering their partner’s goals, but they tended to underestimate the ways they got in the way, and those overly positive self-views were linked to poorer relationship outcomes. This research was published in Journal of Social and Personal Relationships .

People’s personal goals are often shaped by their closest relationships. A partner can make a goal easier to pursue by offering encouragement, joining in, creating time or space, or just not making the goal harder. But partners can also obstruct each other’s goals, sometimes directly and sometimes unintentionally, through competing needs, conflicting routines, or everyday frictions.

This is significant because goal progress is associated with well-being, and romantic partners’ goal systems often become intertwined. Emily Connard and colleagues examined whether people can accurately recognize their own influence on their partner’s daily goals. The authors were especially interested in whether people show “tracking accuracy,” meaning their self-perceptions correspond with their partner’s reports, and whether they also show bias, such as assuming that they affect their partner in the same way their partner affects them.

The study also examined whether these misperceptions carry relational costs. Seeing oneself too positively might protect a person from discomfort, especially when acknowledging obstruction could feel threatening. items.t: People tend to underestimate how much they get in the way of their partner’s goals

items.title: A lipsmacking journey from kisses galore to tears of despair – How Do We Find Love? review
items.summary:
Sainsbury Museum and Art Centre, Norwich
With some uplifting works despite a certain obviousness, this broad double-hander tackles the vast topics of love, smooching and the aftermath

To quote 1980s soft rockers Foreigner, I want to know what love is. And I want the Sainsbury Centre to show me. This big winter series tackles love in all its guises – and for now comprises two shows, one about smooching called The Last Human Kiss, another about desire and heartbreak called Ecstasy and the Aftermath.

The problem is, love is probably the biggest topic in human history, let alone art history. Think of the endless novels and poems and films; think of how many songs have been written, how many paintings painted. Love is an endlessly vast topic and this show barely scratches its surface.
